brief:
- the first paragraph under the new heading "The Parent You Inherited", right after Joel's paragraph that ends "So, it's worth meditating first on why it feels fake."
- what it says: one place to look is the parent you inherited, the way you learned to treat yourself from how people treated you growing up. It was there long before you started building the Nurturer, Protector and Guide. It can be warm, but a lot of the time it's more like a critic, or a warden with rules. Where it was like that, bit by bit your little one learned to keep whatever those rules didn't allow out of sight, so they could keep belonging.
- Nine drafts of this paragraph were flagged as AI by the detector. They all copied the guide's list of five rules and its "for some people it's warm, for a lot of people it's a critic" pair. So: don't list rules. If you give one, give one, in your own words, the way a grown-up might actually say it to a kid. No "for some people / for a lot of people" pair.
- The hiding belongs to the critic or warden case, not to every reader. Don't say "parts of themselves" (this article uses "part" for an inner position). Don't name it "the inherited critic voice", don't point back to earlier sections, and put no doubts or memories in Joel's mouth.
length: three to five sentences, 55 to 95 words
guide_passage: Before you deliberately build the Nurturer, Protector, and Guide, you usually already have a learned way of treating yourself: the inner parent “script” you inherited from how you were treated. It may show up as words, feelings, expectations, or habits rather than a literal inner voice. It can be warm, but for many people its first version is a critic or warden: don’t cry, don’t be needy, don’t get angry, don’t embarrass us, don’t become too independent. Piece by piece, the child learns which qualities have to disappear from view to preserve belonging.
next: The inherited parent compares the outward persona with an impossible ideal, then attacks from both sides: you aren’t good enough, and whatever looks good is fake anyway. No wonder the inner child doesn’t immediately answer when a new adult voice appears and says, “Trust me.”
voice: in the second person like the article, with Joel's first person only for what he thinks now (no claims about his past)
cut: So, it's worth meditating first on why it feels fake.
